segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So, I want us to run through the forms of haber, this to have that we use to go into the past.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: We said that we can remember them by looking at the two vowel sounds that we have inside the word haber. So give me I have and we have.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: He and hemos.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. And give me the rest of the versions.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Ha, has, han.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: We said that nouns ending -a are feminine nouns.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So, for example, the house: la casa.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So, words ending -a are feminine, but words ending -ma are masculine.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: There's a small group of words that end -ma which are masculine words. For example, the problem in Spanish is el problema.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: El problema.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. How would you say have you understood the problem? Have you understood the problem? What was to understand?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Comprender.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Comprender, good. We can use comprender, or we can use entender, but comprender is perfect here as well. Have you understood the problem, and let's talk formally to usted.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: ¿Ha entendido el problema?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. ¿Ha entendido el problema? Good.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So, a very common error for people learning Spanish is to say la problema.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Now, if we look at why these words ending -ma are actually masculine, it's going to help us internalize it.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So, these words that end -ma actually come from Greek. 'Problema' in Greek is 'provlima'.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: 'System' in Greek is 'systima'.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: In Spanish, it's sistema.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So how would you say the system?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: El sistema.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: El sistema. So it's el. Now in Greek, these words are neuter words. In Greek you have masculine, feminine, and neuter. And neuter words in Greek look like masculine words. They have a similar word for the. They look kind of like masculine words. So when they went into Spanish or into Latin, they got mistaken as masculine words.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So if we can identify them, there's a key group of words we can avoid committing this error with. If it ends -ma, it's probably from Greek and probably masculine. So how would you say the system again?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: El sistema.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: El sistema.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: How would you say have you understood the system, talking informally? Have you understood the system?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: ¿Has entendido el sistema?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. ¿Has entendido el sistema? Good.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Sentir in Spanish, sentir, is to feel, related to sensation. So sentir, to feel.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: And you can also use it like to perceive in the sense of smell. So if you wanted to ask, for example, have you felt the aroma, it would be a way of asking have you smelled the aroma, have you felt it? So how would you say that: have you felt the aroma?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: ¿Has sentido el aroma?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. ¿Has sentido el aroma? Good. So el again. So we have el el problema, el sistema, el programa, el aroma, el panorama,

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: el clima, which is a little bit different in English, which means climate, el clima, and some others. Have you understood the program?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: ¿Has entendido el programa?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Again, how was to lose? Perishable.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Perdir.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Close.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Perder.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Perder. Good.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So how would you say I have lost?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: He perdido.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Now, what if you wanted to emphasize I have lost?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Yo he perdido.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Now, if you want to say I have got lost, I've got lost, you can just say I've lost myself.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: We said that I get ready is I prepare myself: me preparo. We don't use this in Spanish 'I get ready'. You say I ready myself, me preparo. So you don't say I get lost or I have got lost, you say I have lost myself. So how would you say that?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Me he perdido.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Again?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Me he perdido.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Yes, when you say it fluently, it doesn't actually sound any different, which is why I asked for it again to make sure that you were putting it, because the 'e' of 'me' and the 'e' of 'he' will blend together: me he perdido, uh?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So that means I have lost myself, or I've got lost.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Now, what if you wanted to be emphatic as well, and say I have lost myself?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Yo me he perdido.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Yo me he perdido. How is you have lost, speaking informally?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Has perdido.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Has perdido. We said that the word for you, in the sense of you lose, you see, not I see you, but you see, is tú for informal you. Tú, T-U.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Tú.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So how would you say you have lost, being emphatic?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Tú ha perdido.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: There's a bit of a contradiction there.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Tú has perdido.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Tú has perdido. Good.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So just as me can mean me or myself, te can mean you or yourself.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So how would you say you have got lost, you have lost yourself?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Te has perdido.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Te has perdido. Te has perdido. And what if you wanted to be emphatic as well?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Tú te has perdido.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Tú te has perdido. Very good.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: What was we have from haber?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Hemos.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Hemos. Good.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: How would you say we have lost it? We have lost it?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Lo hemos perdido.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Lo hemos perdido.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Now how would you say we have lost ourselves, or we've got lost?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Nos hemos perdido.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Nos hemos perdido. And what if you wanted to say we have got lost, we have lost ourselves?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Nosotros nos hemos perdido.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Nosotros nos hemos perdido. Good.
